key_concept: In Rutherford (Geiger–Marsden) scattering the number of $\alpha$-particles scattered at angle $\theta$ varies as $N(\theta) \propto \dfrac{1}{\sin^4(\theta/2)}$, so it is very large at small angles and falls steeply with increasing angle.
steps: Most $\alpha$-particles pass far from the tiny nucleus, so they are deflected only slightly. Very few come close enough to be scattered through large angles.
Small angles: as $\theta \to 0$, $\sin(\theta/2) \to 0$, so $N(\theta)$ becomes very large (around $10^7$ on the graph).

Large angles: at $\theta = 180^\circ$, $\sin^4(90^\circ) = 1$, which is the minimum of $N(\theta)$. Compare with $\theta = 10^\circ$: $\sin^4(5^\circ) \approx (0.087)^4 \approx 5.8\times10^{-5}$, so $N(10^\circ)/N(180^\circ) \approx 1.7\times10^4$.
The curve therefore falls steeply at small angles and flattens near its minimum as $\theta \to 180^\circ$. It is monotonically decreasing with no maximum in between.
Only graph (3) shows this shape: near $10^7$ at very small $\theta$, a sharp drop, then a flat tail at a low value up to $180^\circ$.
final_answer: Option (3): Graph of $N(\theta)$ (log scale, 10 to $10^7$) vs $\theta$ (0 to 180 degrees): curve starting near $10^7$ at very small angle, falling steeply and then flattening out to a low value near $10^2$ at large angles up to $180^\circ$.
why_not_others: Graph (1) shows $N$ increasing with $\theta$, and graph (4) peaks at $90^\circ$; both contradict the observation that large-angle scattering is rare. Graph (2) stays nearly flat at small angles and falls slowly, whereas $1/\sin^4(\theta/2)$ is steepest at small angles and flattens near $180^\circ$.
common_trap: Students pick graph (2) because it also 'decreases', missing that the true curve drops most steeply at small angles and levels off at large angles.
time_saving_tip: Recall $N \propto 1/\sin^4(\theta/2)$: the curve must be huge at small $\theta$, monotonically decreasing, steep first and then flat. Only one option has that shape.
